whose error from the exact implementation is bounded by the operator norm as

‖U−UTrotter,1‖=O⁡((L​Λ​t)2r).\displaystyle\left\|U-U_{{\rm Trotter},1}\right\|=O\left(\frac{(L\Lambda t)^{2}}{r}\right). (S18)

Here, LL denotes the number of decomposition for Hamiltonian, rr is the number of repetitions, and Λ=maxl⁡wl\Lambda=\max_{l}w_{l} is the largest coefficient. The higher order product formulae were also invented by Suzuki to improve the scaling with respect to the simulated time tt [48]. For instance, the second order product formula is given by taking ℳ=(w1​H1/2,…,wL−1​HL−1/2,wL​HL,wL−1​HL−1/2,…,w1​H1/2)\mathcal{M}=(w_{1}H_{1}/2,...,w_{L-1}H_{L-1}/2,w_{L}H_{L},w_{L-1}H_{L-1}/2,...,w_{1}H_{1}/2) as

S2​(τ)\displaystyle S_{2}(\tau) :⁣=\displaystyle:= ∏l=1Lexp⁡(wl​Hl​τ/2)​∏l=L1exp⁡(wl​Hl​τ/2),\displaystyle\prod_{l=1}^{L}\exp(w_{l}H_{l}\tau/2)\prod_{l=L}^{1}\exp(w_{l}H_{l}\tau/2), (S19)

and further the 2​k2k-th order product formula is given by the following recursive procedure as

S2​k​(τ)\displaystyle S_{2k}(\tau) :⁣=\displaystyle:= [S2​k−2​(gk​τ)]2​S2​k−2​((1−4​gk)​τ)​[S2​k−2​(gk​τ)]2,\displaystyle[S_{2k-2}(g_{k}\tau)]^{2}S_{2k-2}((1-4g_{k})\tau)[S_{2k-2}(g_{k}\tau)]^{2}, (S20)

where gk=1/(4−41/(2​k−1))​(k>1)g_{k}=1/(4-4^{1/(2k-1)})~(k>1). By taking the time evolution unitary as UTrotter,2​k=(S2​k(−it/r))rU_{{\rm Trotter},2k}=(S_{2k}(-it/r))^{r}, it follows that the error of the Hamiltonian simulation can be given as

‖U−UTrotter,2​k‖=O⁡((L​Λ​t)2​k+1r2​k).\displaystyle\left\|U-U_{{\rm Trotter},2k}\right\|=O\left(\frac{(L\Lambda t)^{2k+1}}{r^{2k}}\right). (S21)

The product formula enables one to systematically improve the error with respect to, e.g., simulation time tt. Meanwhile, when we count the gate complexity on quantum computers, the prefactor suffers from exponential increase with respect to the order kk [46], and therefore is not preferred in practice. An intriguing alternative is to introduce the randomization into the gate compilation [87, 88, 49]. For instance, it has been pointed out that, by randomly permuting the sequence of operators {Hl}\{H_{l}\} in Eq. (S19) for the second-order product formula improves the error dependence on LL [49]. See Table S5 for the comparison on the gate complexity and error scaling.

While the randomized Trotter methods have performed randomization concerning the order of the Pauli rotations, it was proposed by Campbell that we may stochastically choose the Pauli rotations according to their coefficients in the Hamiltonian to suppress the simulation cost for Hamiltonians that are composed of large numbers of Pauli with small coefficients [46]. To be concrete, according to the probability pl=wl/λp_{l}=w_{l}/\lambda where λ:=∑lwl\lambda:=\sum_{l}w_{l}, we choose the Pauli operator HlH_{l} and append the Pauli rotation e−iHlt/re^{-iH_{l}t/r} to the circuit, which is repeated for rr times. It has been shown that the error scaling in such a technique, called the qDRIFT, is given rather by the L1 norm of the coefficients λ\lambda rather than the number of Paulis LL [See Table S5.].

1 TT-count in Trotter-based methods

The error analysis on the Hamiltonian simulation eventually allows one to analyze the cost to perform the phase estimation up to a target energy accuracy ϵ.\epsilon. For instance, Campbell estimated the number of digits mm required to read out the energy with ϵ\epsilon with success probability 1−pf1-p_{f} as [46]

m=log2⁡(ϵ/2​λ)+log2⁡(1pf+1)−2.\displaystyle m=\log_{2}(\epsilon/2\lambda)+\log_{2}\left(\frac{1}{p_{f}}+1\right)-2. (S22)

By optimizing the gate synthesis accuracy for each control-U2jU^{2^{j}} such that the overall gate count is minimized under a fixed total error, one finds that the total number of rotation gates is given as

NRot∼133​λ2ϵ2​((3/2)​pf)3.\displaystyle N_{\rm Rot}\sim 133\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}((3/2)p_{f})^{3}}. (S23)

While this analysis assumes to run the QPE for a single shot, Lee et al. introduced another layer of “randomization” [12]; by running the phase estimation multiple times, one may sample from the somewhat erroneous probability distribution, whose error can be efficiently suppressed by the Hodges-Lehman estimator to deal with the fat-tail errors. By assuming that the error in the output is symmetric, one obtains the improved number of rotations as

NRot=35.5192​λ2ϵ2.\displaystyle N_{\rm Rot}=35.5192\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}. (S24)

Given the number of rotations, one may estimate the TT-count by multiplying with the gate synthesis cost for controlled rotations. See Table S6 for the summary of the cost required to perform the phase estimation. Note that we also perform a similar analysis in the case of the 2nd order random Trotterization.

4 Post-Trotter Hamiltonian simulation methods for quantum phase estimation

One of the main bottlenecks of the Trotter-based Hamiltonian simulation techniques is that their gate complexity is polynomial regarding the dynamics simulation accuracy δHS\delta_{\rm HS}. Although one may in principle improve the gate-depth scaling as O(δHS−1/2k)O(\delta_{\rm HS}^{-1/2k}) by employing 2​k2k-th order product formulas, one must pay the cost of significantly increased prefactor, which practically negates the advantage of the scaling in moderate-size problems. This has been recognized as roadblock that prevents us from achieving quantum advantage in a practical sense.

A class of Hamiltonian simulation techniques that achieves exponential improvement with respect to the accuracy δHS\delta_{\rm HS} is called the “post-Trotter methods.” While Trotter-based methods mainly consist of exponentiated Pauli rotations that act on the system qubits, in post-Trotter methods the class of available operations on the target system is vastly extended to include even non-unitary operations by making use of an extended Hilbert space. This technique is dubbed as block-encoding. For instance, Ref. [50, 51] proposed an algorithm that block-encodes the truncated Taylor series for the time evolution operator. The gate complexity to perform the phase estimation based on this so-called Taylorization method for lattice systems with size NN with energy accuracy ϵ\epsilon is L​λϵ​log⁡(N/δHS)/log⁡log⁡(N/δHS)\frac{L\lambda}{\epsilon}\log(N/\delta_{\rm HS})/\log\log(N/\delta_{\rm HS}) [89]. A major innovation pointed out by Refs. [90, 91] after the proposal of Taylorization is that one may completely eliminate the Trotter or Taylor errors in phase estimation by simulating ei​arccos⁡(H/λ)e^{i\arccos(H/\lambda)} instead of ei​H​t/λe^{iHt/\lambda}. This idea has been combined with the concept of qubitization [41] to achieve even more efficient implementation of phase estimation algorithm [92]. As we later describe more in detail in Sec. 2, we construct oracles such that the operation of the block-encoding unitary can be “qubitized” into a direct sum of two-dimensional subspace. Each of such “single-qubit rotation” encodes the eigenvalue of the target operator, and therefore can be directly plugged in as a phase estimation subroutine.

In the following, we first introduce the concept of block encoding and its two core subroutines PREPARE and SELECT. Then, we further introduce the qubitization and Taylorization algorithms, which are two representative post-Trotter methods to perform Hamiltonian simulation for phase estimation.

1 Block encoding for linear combination of unitaries

It is instructive to start from the definition of the term block encoding. Let us define that block encoding of some bounded-norm target operator A∈Md​(ℂ)A\in M_{d}(\mathbb{C}) (dd: Hilbert space dimension) is realized when the action of an unitary operator in an extended Hilbert space V∈Md+da​(ℂ)V\in M_{d+d_{a}}(\mathbb{C}) (dad_{a}: auxiliary Hilbert space dimension) reproduces AA at specific subspace. For concreteness, let us consider nn-qubit target system with aa ancillary qubits. We say that “AA is block-encoded into VV via signal state |ℒ⟩\ket{\mathcal{L}}” if the following holds:

(⟨ℒ|⊗I⊗n)​V​(|ℒ⟩⊗I⊗n)=A,\displaystyle(\bra{\mathcal{L}}\otimes I^{\otimes n})V(\ket{\mathcal{L}}\otimes I^{\otimes n})=A,~ (S25)

where |ℒ⟩\ket{\mathcal{L}} is a state in auxiliary aa-qubit Hilbert space and II denotes the identity. Note that we have assumed that ‖A‖≤1\|A\|\leq 1 without loss of generality, since we can rescale the operator as A/α⁡(α∈ℝ)A/\alpha~(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}) if needed. While we may also consider block encoding under multiple signal states as Π​V​Π=A\Pi V\Pi=A where Π=∑ℒΠℒ=∑ℒ|ℒ⟩​⟨ℒ|\Pi=\sum_{\mathcal{L}}\Pi_{\mathcal{L}}=\sum_{\mathcal{L}}\ket{\mathcal{L}}\bra{\mathcal{L}}, here we focus on Eq. (S25) for simplicity. It is illustrative to take |ℒ⟩=|0⟩⊗a\ket{\mathcal{L}}=\ket{0}^{\otimes a} and rewrite Eq. (S25) into an equivalent expression that holds for any target state:

V\displaystyle V =\displaystyle= (A∗∗),\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}A&*\\ &*\\ \end{array}\right),

Observe from Eq. (1) why the technique is called “block-encoding.” Since we can obtain the desired operation A​|ψ⟩A\ket{\psi} with finite probability by post-selecting the measured ancillary qubits to be |0⟩⊗a\ket{0}^{\otimes a}, this is also referred to as “probabilistic implementation of AA.” In reality, we design the algorithm (e.g. use amplitude amplification) so that post selection is not explicitly required.

In phase estimation algorithm based on post-Trotter methods, one aims to extract information on the eigenspectra by making multiple queries to the oracular unitary which block-encodes the Hamiltonian. The underlying assumption is that, there is a systematic and efficient way to encode the spectral information of the Hamiltonian into the oracular unitary VV. As we later observe in the algorithms such as the qubitization and Taylorization, this question essentially falls into the problem of implementing two oracular subroutines named PREPARE and SELECT efficiently. Roughly speaking, PREPARE takes the ancillary quantum state to the properly block-encoded subspace, and SELECT performs the block encoding of the Hamiltonian in the subspace given by the first oracle PREPARE.

To explicitly write down the operation by two subroutines, first, let us note that any operator AA can be decomposed into a linear combination of unitaries as

A\displaystyle A =\displaystyle= ∑lwl​Al​(wl>0),\displaystyle\sum_{l}w_{l}A_{l}~~(w_{l}>0), (S29)

where wlw_{l} is a real positive coefficient of the unitary operator AlA_{l}. For nn-qubit systems, AlA_{l} can be thought to be a tensor product of multiple Pauli operators with arbitrary complex phase. The first oracle PREPARE is often introduced to perform the following transformation that encodes all LL coefficients of the Hamiltonian into the ancillary qubits as

|ℒ⟩:=𝙿𝚁𝙴𝙿𝙰𝚁𝙴​|0⟩⊗a\displaystyle\ket{\mathcal{L}}:={\tt PREPARE}\ket{0}^{\otimes a} =\displaystyle= ∑l=1Lwlλ​|l⟩,\displaystyle\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sqrt{\frac{w_{l}}{\lambda}}\ket{l}, (S30)

where λ=∑lwl\lambda=\sum_{l}w_{l} is the L1L_{1} norm of the coefficients of Hamiltonian. Given the orthogonal bases {|l⟩}l\{\ket{l}\}_{l} that encodes the information of the coefficients, next we construct the second oracle SELECT so that the desired operator AA is realized in the subspace as

(⟨ℒ|⊗I)​𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃​(|ℒ⟩⊗I)=Aλ.\displaystyle(\bra{\mathcal{L}}\otimes I){\tt SELECT}(\ket{\mathcal{L}}\otimes I)=\frac{A}{\lambda}. (S31)

While the construction of SELECT oracle is not unique, it is instructive to introduce an example as follows:

𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃\displaystyle{\tt SELECT} =\displaystyle= ∑l|l⟩​⟨l|⊗Al+∑l¯|l¯⟩​⟨l¯|⊗I,\displaystyle\sum_{l}\ket{l}\bra{l}\otimes A_{l}+\sum_{\bar{l}}\ket{\bar{l}}\bra{\bar{l}}\otimes I, (S32)

where we have introduced l¯\bar{l} to denote computational bases of ancillary qubit system on which SELECT acts trivially.

2 Qubitization

Ref.  [41] pointed out that, by choosing the operator AA in Eq. (S29) to be the Hamiltonian of the target system, one may construct a unitary that invokes rotational operation for each eigenstates. Since all the rotation is performed disjointly on two-dimensional subspace, such a specific form of block encoding is referred to as the qubitization.

Let A=∑χχ​|χ⟩​⟨χ|A=\sum_{\chi}\chi\ket{\chi}\bra{\chi} be a target Hermitian operator which we wish to block-encode into the SELECT operator via the signal state |ℒ⟩=𝙿𝚁𝙴𝙿𝙰𝚁𝙴​|0⟩\ket{\mathcal{L}}={\tt PREPARE}\ket{0} as in Eq.  (S30), (S32), (S31). To understand the “qubitized” picture, we focus on a single eigenstate |χ⟩\ket{\chi}, and also introduce an orthogonal state |⟂χ⟩=11−χ2​(𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃−χ​I)​|ℒ⟩​|χ⟩\ket{\perp_{\chi}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\chi^{2}}}({\tt SELECT}-\chi I)\ket{\mathcal{L}}\ket{\chi} so that

𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃​|ℒ⟩​|χ⟩=χ​|ℒ⟩​|χ⟩+1−χ2​|⟂χ⟩.\displaystyle{\tt SELECT}\ket{\mathcal{L}}\ket{\chi}=\chi\ket{\mathcal{L}}\ket{\chi}+\sqrt{1-\chi^{2}}\ket{\perp_{\chi}}. (S33)

We say that the oracles are qubitized if the action of the SELECT is closed within the two-dimensional subspace ℋχ=Span⁡(|ℒ⟩​|χ⟩,|⟂χ⟩)\mathcal{H}_{\chi}={\rm Span}(\ket{\mathcal{L}}\ket{\chi},\ket{\perp_{\chi}}), which is known to be satisfied if and only if ⟨ℒ|𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃2|ℒ⟩=I\braket{\mathcal{L}|{\tt SELECT}^{2}|\mathcal{L}}=I [41]. Observe that SELECT defined as Eq. (S32) satisfies this condition; AA is now Hermitian and hence can be decomposed as A=∑lwl​AlA=\sum_{l}w_{l}A_{l} with wl>0w_{l}>0 and Al2=IA_{l}^{2}=I. Meanwhile, this does not hold if AA is not Hermitian (as in the case of truncated Taylor series of unitary time evolution operator). We find that other transition amplitudes can be computed explicitly as

⟨ℒ|​⟨χ|​𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃​|⟂χ⟩\displaystyle\bra{\mathcal{L}}\bra{\chi}{\tt SELECT}\ket{\perp_{\chi}} =\displaystyle= ⟨ℒ|​⟨χ|​𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃​(𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃−χ​I)​|ℒ⟩​|χ⟩/1−χ2\displaystyle\bra{\mathcal{L}}\bra{\chi}{\tt SELECT}({\tt SELECT}-\chi I)\ket{\mathcal{L}}\ket{\chi}/\sqrt{1-\chi^{2}} (S34)
=\displaystyle= 1−χ21−χ2=1−χ2,\displaystyle\frac{1-\chi^{2}}{\sqrt{1-\chi^{2}}}=\sqrt{1-\chi^{2}}, (S35)
⟨⟂χ|𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃|⟂χ⟩\displaystyle\braket{\perp_{\chi}|{\tt SELECT}|\perp_{\chi}} =\displaystyle= ⟨ℒ|​⟨χ|​(𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃−χ​I)​𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃​(𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃−χ​I)​|ℒ⟩​|χ⟩/(1−χ2)\displaystyle\bra{\mathcal{L}}\bra{\chi}({\tt SELECT}-\chi I){\tt SELECT}({\tt SELECT}-\chi I)\ket{\mathcal{L}}\ket{\chi}/(1-\chi^{2}) (S36)
=\displaystyle= ⟨ℒ|​⟨χ|​(𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃−2​χ​I+χ2​𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃)​|ℒ⟩​|χ⟩/(1−χ2)\displaystyle\bra{\mathcal{L}}\bra{\chi}({\tt SELECT}-2\chi I+\chi^{2}{\tt SELECT})\ket{\mathcal{L}}\ket{\chi}/(1-\chi^{2}) (S37)
=\displaystyle= −χ⁡(1−χ2)1−1​χ2=−χ,\displaystyle\frac{-\chi(1-\chi^{2})}{1-1\chi^{2}}=-\chi, (S38)

and therefore the action within the effective Hilbert space HχH_{\chi} is given as follows:

𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃χ=(χ1−χ21−χ2−χ).\displaystyle{\tt SELECT}_{\chi}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\chi&\sqrt{1-\chi^{2}}\\ \sqrt{1-\chi^{2}}&-\chi\\ \end{array}\right).

Observe that the action satisfies 𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃χ​𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃χ†=I{\tt SELECT}_{\chi}{\tt SELECT}_{\chi}^{\dagger}=I and indeed closed within the subspace.

The framework of the qubitization enables one to perform a vast class of polynomial transformation on the eigenspectrum of AA as Poly⁡(A){\rm Poly}(A). This implies that, one can build up a new block encoding of an operator from an existing block encoded operator, just as one develops a new algorithm by combining subroutines [93]. For instance, given a block encoding of AA, one may construct a block encoding of polynomial approximation for ei​Ae^{iA} , from which one may also derive a block encoding of A−1A^{-1}. Such a methodology to manipulate eigenvalues enable one to extract various information from the block encoded operator.

Now we have confirmed that the oracles defined as in Eqs. (S30),  (S32) are readily qubitized. Let us next proceed to construct a Szegedy-type walk opeartor as 𝒲=ℛℒ⋅𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃\mathcal{W}=\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{L}}\cdot{\tt SELECT}, which combines 𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃{\tt SELECT} with another reflection operator defined as ℛℒ=2​|ℒ⟩​⟨ℒ|−I\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{L}}=2\ket{\mathcal{L}}\bra{\mathcal{L}}-I. It is straightforward to find that 𝒲\mathcal{W} is also qubitized in each two-dimensional subspace ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k} which is defined from the kk-th eigenstate of the Hamiltonian:

𝒲k=(Ek/λ1−(Ek/λ)2−1−(Ek/λ)2Ek/λ)=ei​arccos⁡(Ek/λ)​Y,\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{k}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}E_{k}/\lambda&\sqrt{1-(E_{k}/\lambda)^{2}}\\ -\sqrt{1-(E_{k}/\lambda)^{2}}&E_{k}/\lambda\\ \end{array}\right)=e^{i\arccos(E_{k}/\lambda)Y},

where EkE_{k} denotes the kk-th eigenenergy. Therefore, this walk operator not only block-encodes the Hamiltonian in the signal space as ⟨ℒ|𝒲|ℒ⟩=ei​arccos⁡(H/λ)\braket{\mathcal{L}|\mathcal{W}|\mathcal{L}}=e^{i\arccos(H/\lambda)}, but also provides efficient access to its entire eigenspectra.

Using the oracles PREPARE and SELECT introduced above, we construct the entire circuit as shown in Fig. S10, where we have also introduced the preparation circuit for the readout qubits as [92]

χm​|0⟩m=22m+1​∑i=02m−1sin⁡(π⁡(i+1)2m+1)​|i⟩.\displaystyle\chi_{m}\ket{0}^{m}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{2^{m}+1}}\sum_{i=0}^{2^{m}-1}\sin\left(\frac{\pi(i+1)}{2^{m}+1}\right)\ket{i}. (S45)

This consumes TT-gates of O~​(m)\tilde{O}(m) and hence neglected in the resource analysis in the present work. It is crucial to the resource estimate that the number of readout digits mm is determined from the number of repetition rr regarding the the quantum walk operations as [94, 95, 12]

r=⌈π​λ2​ϵ⌉<2m.\displaystyle r=\left\lceil\frac{\pi\lambda}{2\epsilon}\right\rceil<2^{m}. (S46)

This leads us to obtain the relation between the cost (i.e., TT-count or detailed runtime) of the global algorithm and the oracles as

CHS∼r×(CP+CP†+CS+2​Cℛ0),\displaystyle C_{\rm HS}\sim r\times(C_{\rm P}+C_{{\rm P}^{\dagger}}+C_{\rm S}+2C_{\mathcal{R}_{0}}), (S47)

where CP(†)C_{{\rm P}^{({\dagger})}} and CSC_{\rm S} denote the cost required for the PREPARE and SELECT oracles, respectively, and Cℛ0C_{\mathcal{R}_{0}} is the cost for the reflection by |0⟩|0\rangle. By explicitly constructing the quantum circuits as shown in Sec. S5, we find that the cost for ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0} and 𝙿𝚁𝙴𝙿𝙰𝚁𝙴{\tt PREPARE}, which is only logarithmic with system size, indeed become asymptotically negligible (See Fig. S11).

3 Taylorization

Taylorization is one of the earliest attempts to overcome the polynomial gate complexity Poly⁡(1/δHS){\rm Poly}(1/\delta_{\rm HS}) in Trotter-based Hamiltonian simulation methods [90, 91]. In essence, the algorithm uses the technique of block encoding to approximate the time evolution operator U=exp⁡(−i​A​t)U=\exp(-iAt) with the repetitive operation of truncated Taylor series up to KK-th order (See Fig. S12), which results in polylog⁡(1/δHS){\rm polylog}(1/\delta_{\rm HS}) gate complexity. To be concrete, the time evolution is divided into rr steps as U=(Ur)rU=(U_{r})^{r} with Ur=exp(−iAt/r)U_{r}=\exp(-iAt/r), where each step is approximated as

U~r\displaystyle\widetilde{U}_{r} :⁣=\displaystyle:= ∑k=0K(−iAt/r)kk!Hk=∑k=0K∑l1,…,lkwl1⋯wlKAl1⋯AlK.\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{K}\frac{(-iAt/r)^{k}}{k!}H^{k}=\sum_{k=0}^{K}\sum_{l_{1},...,l_{k}}w_{l_{1}}\cdots w_{l_{K}}A_{l_{1}}\cdots A_{l_{K}}. (S48)

Hyperparameters such as KK and rr shall be chosen in order to predict the output energy with target precision ϵ\epsilon. Following the discussion of the qubitization and also Ref. [51, 96], we take

r=π2​δP​E​A(∼π​λ2​ϵ),K=⌈−1+2​log⁡(2​r/δHS)log⁡log⁡(2​r/δHS)+1⌉,\displaystyle r=\frac{\pi}{2\delta_{PEA}}~\left(\sim\frac{\pi\lambda}{2\epsilon}\right),\ \ \ K=\left\lceil-1+\frac{2\log(2r/\delta_{\rm HS})}{\log\log(2r/\delta_{\rm HS})+1}\right\rceil, (S49)

where λ=∑lwl\lambda=\sum_{l}w_{l} is the total sum of coefficients for A=∑lwl​AlA=\sum_{l}w_{l}A_{l}. Note that the scaling of O⁡(1/ϵ)O(1/\epsilon) reflects the time-energy uncertainty relation in order to extract the eigenstate energy.

Once we construct PREPARE and SELECT for truncated Taylor series Eq. (S48), we find that the block encoding is realized via a walk operator

W:=(𝙿𝚁𝙴𝙿𝙰𝚁𝙴†)​(𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃)​(𝙿𝚁𝙴𝙿𝙰𝚁𝙴),\displaystyle W:=({\tt PREPARE}^{\dagger})({\tt SELECT})({\tt PREPARE}), (S50)

whose explicit operation is given using s=∑k=0K∑l1,…,lKwl1⋯wlKs=\sum_{k=0}^{K}\sum_{l_{1},...,l_{K}}w_{l_{1}}\cdots w_{l_{K}} as

W​|0⟩​|ψ⟩=1s​|0⟩​U~r​|ψ⟩+1−1s2​|⟂⟩.\displaystyle W\ket{0}\ket{\psi}=\frac{1}{s}\ket{0}\widetilde{U}_{r}\ket{\psi}+\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{s^{2}}}\ket{\perp}. (S51)

Although the unwanted second term seem to deteriorate the simulation, we may tune the amplitude of the target state via the oblivious amplitude estimation introduced in  [50]. Namely, we rescale the time evolution as s=2s=2 so that the combination of the walk operator and a reflection operator on the ancillary qubits ℛ0=I−2​|0⟩​⟨0|\mathcal{R}_{0}=I-2\ket{0}\bra{0} gives [51]

W​ℛ0​W†​ℛ0​W​|0⟩​|ψ⟩=−|0⟩​U~​|ψ⟩.\displaystyle W\mathcal{R}_{0}W^{\dagger}\mathcal{R}_{0}W\ket{0}\ket{\psi}=-\ket{0}\widetilde{U}\ket{\psi}. (S52)

Finally, by plugging the controlled operation of U~\widetilde{U} into the quantum circuit of phase estimation, we obtain the circuit structure of the entire algorithm as in Fig. S12. The overall cost is given as follows,

CHS∼r×(3​(CP+CP†+CS)+2​Cℛ0),\displaystyle C_{\rm HS}\sim r\times(3(C_{\rm P}+C_{{\rm P}^{\dagger}}+C_{\rm S})+2C_{\mathcal{R}_{0}}), (S53)

where CPC_{\rm P} and CSC_{\rm S} is obtained from KK-fold multiplication on cost for the qubitization algorithm, while Cℛ0C_{\mathcal{R}_{0}} is simply the cost for multi-controlled Z-gate operated on ancillas. In practice, the number of repetitions rr is around tens of thousands (see also Sec. S9) and KK is around 30 to 40 for the target models with system size of above hundreds. This indicates that each unit oracles are executed for 105−610^{5-6} times.

S5 Post-Trotter oracles for lattice models

In Sec. 4, we have introduced the technique of block encoding, which allows us to perform Hamiltonian simulation with gate complexity that scales polylogarithmically with respect to the target accuracy δHS\delta_{\rm HS}. In this section, we further provide the explicit construction of quantum circuits that cover a broad range of lattice models considered in condensed matter physics. We introduce two methods to construct oracles, which we refer to as sequential and product-wise constructions.

The sequential construction is designed to block-encode each Pauli operators one by one. Given LL terms, we use ⌈log⁡L⌉\lceil\log L\rceil ancillary qubits for 𝙿𝚁𝙴𝙿𝙰𝚁𝙴{\tt PREPARE} oracle, so that ll-th computational basis is used to block-encode the ll-th Pauli operator PlP_{l} by the 𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃{\tt SELECT} oracle. On the other hand, the core idea of product-wise structure is utilize the translational symmetric structure of the connectivity; we encode the information on local connectivity and the interaction amplitude into PREPARE oracle, while we keep SELECT rather agnostic to the geometry. Such a construction turns out to be beneficial compared to the sequential one when the connectivity is dense; for instance, when we have all-to-all GG-local interaction, the gate complexity drops from O⁡(NG)O(N^{G}) to O⁡(G​N)O(GN) [97].

In the following, abstract descriptions are provided each for PREPARE and SELECT oracles in Secs. 1 and 2, respectively. Subsequently we give constructions for quantum spin models and fermionic models whose interaction is geometrically local and translationally invariant. Then, we proceed to show examples in concrete models: spin-1/2 J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model and Fermi-Hubbard model on the square lattice, and also the spin-1 Heisenberg chain. From the results of TT-count analysis combined with that for Trotter-based methods presented in Sec. 3, we compare the order of computational cost between various phase estimation subroutines to conclude that the qubitization algorithm gives the best practice among the Hamiltonian simulation subroutines. We further guide readers to Sec. S8 for more detailed runtime analysis that compiles quantum circuit of the qubitization algorithm into executable instructions. We importantly remark that we have chosen the product-wise construction to the compare TT-counts between Hamiltonian simulation subroutines, while the for the runtime analysis we focus on the sequential type of SELECT oracle for the sake of simplicity.

1 Abstract structure of PREPARE

Here, we present the abstract structure of PREPARE circuit that achieves polylogamithmic cost, in terms of both TT-count and ancillary qubit count, for translationally-invariant GG-local Hamiltonians introduced in Sec. S1 as

H=∑𝒑∑{𝝁,𝜶}w𝝁,𝜶Λ^𝒑(𝜶)Λ^𝒑+𝝁1(𝜶)⋯Λ^𝒑+𝝁G−1(𝜶),\displaystyle H=\sum_{\bm{p}}\sum_{\{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}\}}w_{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}}\hat{\Lambda}_{\bm{p}}^{(\bm{\alpha})}\hat{\Lambda}_{\bm{p}+\bm{\mu}_{1}}^{(\bm{\alpha})}\cdots\hat{\Lambda}_{\bm{p}+\bm{\mu}_{G-1}}^{(\bm{\alpha})}, (S54)

where 𝒑=(p1,…,pd)\bm{p}=(p_{1},\dots,p_{d}) labels the site (including the sublattice structure), 𝝁=(𝝁1,…,𝝁G−1)\bm{\mu}=(\bm{\mu}_{1},...,\bm{\mu}_{G-1}) is a set of vectors that identifies the connection between interacting sites, Λ^𝒑𝜶\hat{\Lambda}^{\bm{\alpha}}_{\bm{p}} is an operator for microscopic degrees of freedom (e.g. spin, fermion, boson) on site 𝒑\bm{p}, and w𝝁,𝜶w_{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}} is the amplitude of the interaction. As we display in Fig. S13, both the PREPARE for qubitization and Taylorization consist of the identical subroutine which we call in this paper as UNIT-PREP. Therefore, let us first focus on the case of qubitization and later mention the case of Taylorization.

First we introduce the sequential construction, which straightforwardly encodes all the information of coefficients as

𝚄𝙽𝙸𝚃​-​𝙿𝚁𝙴𝙿:|0⟩↦|ℒ⟩=∑𝒑∑{𝝁,𝜶}w𝝁,𝜶λ​|𝒑⟩​|𝝁,𝜶⟩.\displaystyle{\tt UNIT}\text{-}{\tt PREP}:\ket{0}\mapsto\ket{\mathcal{L}}=\sum_{\bm{p}}\sum_{\{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}\}}\sqrt{\frac{w_{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}}}{\lambda}}\ket{\bm{p}}\ket{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}}. (S55)

Thanks to the translational invariance of the Hamiltonian, we may split the ancilla for geometrical position 𝒑\bm{p} and interaction configurations 𝝁,𝜶\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}. Note that in the graphical description in Fig. S14(a) we have introduced 𝚄𝙽𝙸𝙵𝙾𝚁𝙼N​|0⟩=1N​∑n=1N|n⟩{\tt UNIFORM}_{N}\ket{0}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\ket{n}.

One evident difference between the product-wise construction from the sequential one is the GG-fold increase in use of ancilla qubits, from which we benefit in terms of TT-count in SELECT oracle (See. 2). The general form of product-wise UNIT-PREP encodes the interaction amplitudes into ancillary qubits as follows:

𝚄𝙽𝙸𝚃​-​𝙿𝚁𝙴𝙿:|0⟩↦|ℒ⟩=∑𝒑∑{𝝁,𝜶}w𝝁,𝜶λ​|𝒑,𝒑+𝝁1,…,𝒑+𝝁G−1⟩​|𝝁,𝜶⟩.\displaystyle{\tt UNIT}\text{-}{\tt PREP}:\ket{0}\mapsto\ket{\mathcal{L}}=\sum_{\bm{p}}\sum_{\{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}\}}\sqrt{\frac{w_{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}}}{\lambda}}\ket{\bm{p},\bm{p}+\bm{\mu}_{1},...,\bm{p}+\bm{\mu}_{G-1}}\ket{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}}. (S56)

As shown in Fig. S14(b), this can roughly be decomposed into three steps as

|0⟩→Rotations(∑𝒑|𝒑⟩​|0⟩(G−1)​log⁡N)⊗(∑{𝝁,𝜶}w𝝁,𝜶​|𝝁,𝜶⟩)=∑𝒑∑{𝝁,𝜶}w𝝁,𝜶​|𝒑⟩​|0⟩(G−1)​log⁡N​|𝝁,𝜶⟩→𝙲𝙾𝙿𝚈​_​𝙸𝙽𝙳𝙴𝚇∑𝒑∑{𝝁,𝜶}w𝝁,𝜶​|𝒑,𝒑,…,𝒑⟩​|𝝁,𝜶⟩→𝚂𝙷𝙸𝙵𝚃​_​𝙸𝙽𝙳𝙴𝚇∑𝒑∑{𝝁,𝜶}w𝝁,𝜶λ​|𝒑,𝒑+𝝁1,…,𝒑+𝝁G−1⟩​|𝝁,𝜶⟩(=|ℒ⟩),\displaystyle\begin{split}\ket{0}&\xrightarrow{\rm Rotations}\left(\sum_{\bm{p}}\ket{\bm{p}}\ket{0}^{(G-1)\log N}\right)\otimes\left(\sum_{\{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}\}}\sqrt{w_{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}}}\ket{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}}\right)=\sum_{\bm{p}}\sum_{\{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}\}}\sqrt{w_{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}}}\ket{\bm{p}}\ket{0}^{(G-1)\log N}\ket{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}}\\ &\xrightarrow{{\tt COPY\_INDEX}}\sum_{\bm{p}}\sum_{\{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}\}}\sqrt{w_{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}}}\ket{\bm{p},\bm{p},...,\bm{p}}\ket{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}}\\ &\xrightarrow{{\tt SHIFT\_INDEX}}\sum_{\bm{p}}\sum_{\{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}\}}\sqrt{\frac{w_{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}}}{\lambda}}\ket{\bm{p},\bm{p}+\bm{\mu}_{1},...,\bm{p}+\bm{\mu}_{G-1}}\ket{\bm{\mu},\bm{\alpha}}(=\ket{\mathcal{L}}),\end{split} (S57)

where NN is the total system size. Note that we have abbreviated overall coefficients in the first and second lines for the sake of simplicity.

The main resource of TT-count is the synthesis of the rotation gates in the first step, and the adder circuit for SHIFT_INDEX (note that COPY_INDEX can be performed solely by CNOT gates). Regarding the dynamics simulation error δHS\delta_{\rm HS}, the order of the TT-count can be obtained as 8​log⁡N+N𝝁,𝜶​log⁡(1/δss)8\log N+N_{{\bm{\mu}},{\bm{\alpha}}}\log(1/\delta_{\rm ss}) where δss=δsyn/r\delta_{\rm ss}=\delta_{\rm syn}/r where the required number of ancillary qubits can be estimated as (G+1)​log⁡N+log⁡N𝜶,𝝁+O⁡(1)(G+1)\log N+\log N_{\bm{\alpha},\bm{\mu}}+O(1), with N𝜶,𝝁=N𝜶​N𝝁N_{\bm{\alpha},\bm{\mu}}=N_{\bm{\alpha}}N_{\bm{\mu}} denoting the total number of combinations of (𝜶,𝝁)(\bm{\alpha},\bm{\mu}). Here, we assume to use the efficient implementation of logical adder that use auxiliary qubits to store the information of “carry-on” [98], resulting in additional use of ancillary qubits of log⁡N𝜶,𝝁\log N_{\bm{\alpha},\bm{\mu}}. Note that, for the PREPARE circuit for Taylorization, we prepare N𝜶,𝝁​log⁡L+log⁡N𝜶,𝝁N_{\bm{\alpha},\bm{\mu}}\log L+\log N_{\bm{\alpha},\bm{\mu}} ancilla qubits to encode information on higher order contribution from Taylor expansion, as can be seen from Fig. S13.

Last but not least, let us mention how to deal with the boundary condition. Be aware that the above-mentioned construction assumes translationally invariant Hamiltonian defined under the periodic boundary condition. However, of course we are not limited to this situation: open, cylinder, or twisted boundary conditions can also be readily treated as well. One straightforward way is to encode the boundary terms individually, which can be done by sparing TT-count of log⁡(Nd−1/d)\log(N^{d-1/d}). However, in this work we consider an alternative method to simulate Hamiltonians defined on cylindrical boundary condition which solely relies on simple postprocessing and rescaling of the Hamiltonian. The details are explained in Sec. S7.

2 Abstract structure of SELECT

Next, we present the sequential and product-wise structure of SELECT oracles that are used to block-encode an operator H=∑l=1Lwl​HlH=\sum_{l=1}^{L}w_{l}H_{l}. In the sequential construction, we perform one-hot encoding of individual unitary HlH_{l} as defined in Eq. (S32) as

𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃=∑l|l⟩​⟨l|⊗Hl+∑l¯|l¯⟩​⟨l¯|⊗I.\displaystyle{\tt SELECT}=\sum_{l}\ket{l}\bra{l}\otimes H_{l}+\sum_{\bar{l}}\ket{\bar{l}}\bra{\bar{l}}\otimes I.~ (S58)

In particular, we assume that every HlH_{l} is a tensor product of Pauli operators (with global phase ±i\pm i or ±1\pm 1) so that we can implement HlH_{l} and controlled HlH_{l} with Clifford operations. Babbush et al. has proposed a quantum circuit that realizes Eq. (S58) with TT-count of 4​L−44L-4 [92], whose structure is explicitly shown in Fig. S15(a).

While Fig. S15(a) is applicable to general form of Hamiltonian, we find that in many cases the translational symmetry allows even more efficient implementation via product-wise construction. The product-wise qubitization is designed so that the (hyper-)connectivity of local terms are encoded solely in PREPARE, while the SELECT oracle is agnostic to the geometric information. Assume that we have PREPARE oracle that generates a signal state

𝙿𝚁𝙴𝙿𝙰𝚁𝙴|0⟩=|ℒ⟩=∑𝜶,𝝁∑𝒑w𝜶,𝝁λ|𝒑1,𝒑1+𝝁1,…,𝒑1+𝝁G−1⟩,\displaystyle{\tt PREPARE}|0\rangle=|\mathcal{L}\rangle=\sum_{{\bm{\alpha}},{\bm{\mu}}}\sum_{{\bm{p}}}\sqrt{\frac{w_{\bm{\alpha},\bm{\mu}}}{\lambda}}|{\bm{p}}_{1},{\bm{p}}_{1}+{\bm{\mu}}_{1},...,{\bm{p}}_{1}+{\bm{\mu}}_{G-1}\rangle, (S59)

using the construction method discussed in the previous subsection. Then, it suffices to construct the SELECT oracle without encoding the information of 𝝁{\bm{\mu}} to block-encode the entire Hamiltonian. Concretely, consider the following operation:

𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃=∑𝜶,𝒑1,…,𝒑G|𝜶⟩⟨𝜶|⊗|𝒑1,…,𝒑G⟩⟨𝒑1,…,𝒑G|⊗H𝒑1(𝜶)H𝒑2(𝜶)⋯H𝒑G(𝜶).\displaystyle{\tt SELECT}=\sum_{{\bm{\alpha}},{\bm{p}}_{1},...,{\bm{p}}_{G}}|{\bm{\alpha}}\rangle\langle{\bm{\alpha}}|\otimes|{\bm{p}}_{1},...,{\bm{p}}_{G}\rangle\langle{\bm{p}}_{1},...,{\bm{p}}_{G}|\otimes H_{{\bm{p}}_{1}}^{(\bm{\alpha})}H_{{\bm{p}}_{2}}^{(\bm{\alpha})}\cdots H_{{\bm{p}}_{G}}^{(\bm{\alpha})}. (S60)

Observe that this satisfies 𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃2=I{\tt SELECT}^{2}=I and the following:

⟨ℒ|𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃|ℒ⟩=∑𝜶,𝝁,𝒑w𝜶,𝝁λH𝒑(𝜶)H𝒑+𝝁2(𝜶)⋯H𝒑+𝝁G−1(𝜶)=H/λ.\displaystyle\langle\mathcal{L}|{\tt SELECT}|\mathcal{L}\rangle=\sum_{{\bm{\alpha}},{\bm{\mu}},{\bm{p}}}\frac{w_{{\bm{\alpha}},{\bm{\mu}}}}{\lambda}H_{{\bm{p}}}^{(\bm{\alpha})}H_{{\bm{p}}+{\bm{\mu}}_{2}}^{(\bm{\alpha})}\cdots H_{{\bm{p}}+{\bm{\mu}}_{G-1}}^{(\bm{\alpha})}=H/\lambda. (S61)

This allows us to block-encode the Hamiltonian with simpler quantum circuit structure. In fact, by observing that Eq. (S60) can be written as tensor product as

𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃=∑𝜶|𝜶⟩⟨𝜶|⊗[(∑𝒑|𝒑1⟩⟨𝒑1|⊗H𝒑1𝜶)⊗(∑𝒑|𝒑2⟩⟨𝒑2|⊗H𝒑2𝜶)⊗⋯⊗(∑𝒑|𝒑G⟩⟨𝒑G|⊗H𝒑G𝜶)],\displaystyle{\tt SELECT}=\sum_{\bm{\alpha}}|\bm{\alpha}\rangle\langle\bm{\alpha}|\otimes\left[\left(\sum_{\bm{p}}|\bm{p}_{1}\rangle\langle\bm{p}_{1}|\otimes H_{\bm{p}_{1}}^{\bm{\alpha}}\right)\otimes\left(\sum_{\bm{p}}|\bm{p}_{2}\rangle\langle\bm{p}_{2}|\otimes H_{\bm{p}_{2}}^{\bm{\alpha}}\right)\otimes\cdots\otimes\left(\sum_{\bm{p}}|\bm{p}_{G}\rangle\langle\bm{p}_{G}|\otimes H_{\bm{p}_{G}}^{\bm{\alpha}}\right)\right], (S62)

it is natural to employ the structure as shown in Fig. S15(b). We find that each “thread” is used to block-encode 2​S​N𝜶​Nsite2SN_{\bm{\alpha}}N_{\rm site} Pauli operators, respectively. Namely, we have G×2​S​N𝜶​NsiteG\times 2SN_{\bm{\alpha}}N_{\rm site} terms in total, and thus the TT-count per 𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃{\tt SELECT} oracle is 4×G×2​S​N𝜶​Nsite−44\times G\times 2SN_{\bm{\alpha}}N_{\rm site}-4 (see Table S8.) For concrete circuit structures of 2d J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model, 2d Fermi-Hubbard model, and spin-SS Heisenberg chain, see Sec. 1, 2, and  3, respectively.

The connectivity-agnostic construction of SELECT oracle turns out to be beneficial in particular when we consider a densely coupled system due to, e.g., high dimensionality or long-range interaction. For instance, let us consider a spin-SS Heisenberg model on dd-dimensional hypercube with rr-nearest-neighbor interaction, each site of which is coupled to γr,d\gamma_{r,d} sites. Under such a procedure, the number of Pauli operator is given as

L=3×(2​S)2×γr,d2×Nsite.\displaystyle L=3\times(2S)^{2}\times\frac{\gamma_{r,d}}{2}\times N_{\rm site}. (S63)

Note the factor 2​S2S due to encoding of high-spin operator as a sum of Pauli operator as Spa=12​∑ν=12​Sσp,νaS_{p}^{a}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\nu=1}^{2S}\sigma_{p,\nu}^{a}. Meanwhile, as we show in Table S8, the product-wise construction of SELECT is not affected by the connectivity of the interaction profile; this gives improvement for arbitrary interaction profile except for the case of spin-1/2 1d nearest-neighbor interaction. Furthermore, when we consider a quantum spin-SS model with all-to-all GG-local interactions, the reduction on the TT-count is even more significant; each sequential-type SELECT oracle requires O⁡(SG​NG)O(S^{G}N^{G}) while the product-wise type can be implemented by O⁡(G​S​N)O(GSN), in exchange for additional O⁡(G​log⁡N)O(G\log N) ancilla qubits. Systematic discussion on such advantage is discussed elsewhere [97].

Let us remark briefly on the estimation of the actual runtime. While we may use TT-counts as the baseline to compare the performance between different Hamiltonian simulation algorithms, we further discuss in Sec. S8 that the actual runtime (which is more related with the TT-depth) can be further improved by distributed implementation of the controlled HlH_{l} operation.

3 Explicit construction of oracles

We are now ready to dive into the explicit construction of quantum circuits for executing post-Trotter methods. Since it is straightforward to modify the circuits generated for qubitization into those for Taylorization, we exclusively discuss the oracles for qubitization.

1 2d J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model

The Hamiltonian of spin-1/2 J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model on the square lattice is defined as in Eq. (S2) as

H=J1​∑⟨p,q⟩∑α∈{X,Y,Z}Spα​Sqα+J2​∑⟨⟨p,q⟩⟩∑α∈{X,Y,Z}Spα​Sqα,\displaystyle H=J_{1}\sum_{\langle p,q\rangle}\sum_{\alpha\in\{X,Y,Z\}}S_{p}^{\alpha}S_{q}^{\alpha}+J_{2}\sum_{\langle\langle p,q\rangle\rangle}\sum_{\alpha\in\{X,Y,Z\}}S_{p}^{\alpha}S_{q}^{\alpha}, (S64)

where the summation of the first and second terms concerns nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor sites, respectively, and SpαS_{p}^{\alpha} is now the spin-1/2 operator. Here we exclusively consider a square lattice of N=M×MN=M\times M sites, and focus on the model with J1=1,J2=0.5J_{1}=1,J_{2}=0.5 where quantum spin liquid phase is expected to show up.

First, let us briefly introduce the sequential construction of UNIT-PREP oracle. The circuit structure shown in Fig. S16(a) realizes the following action:

𝚄𝙽𝙸𝚃​-​𝙿𝚁𝙴𝙿​|0⟩↦∑p∑α∈{X,Y,Z}∑μ=1,2J1λ​|p⟩​|α⟩​|μ⟩+∑μ=3,4J2λ​|p⟩​|α⟩​|μ⟩,\displaystyle\begin{split}{\tt UNIT}\text{-}{\tt PREP}\ket{0}\mapsto\sum_{p}\sum_{\alpha\in\{X,Y,Z\}}\sum_{\mu=1,2}\sqrt{\frac{J_{1}}{\lambda}}\ket{p}\ket{\alpha}\ket{\mu}+\sum_{\mu=3,4}\sqrt{\frac{J_{2}}{\lambda}}\ket{p}\ket{\alpha}\ket{\mu},\end{split} (S65)

where μ∈{1,2,3,4}\mu\in\{1,2,3,4\} correspond to the coupling between (px,py)(p_{x},p_{y}) and (px+1,py),(px,py+1),(px+1,py+1),(px−1,py+1)(p_{x}+1,p_{y}),(p_{x},p_{y}+1),(p_{x}+1,p_{y}+1),(p_{x}-1,p_{y}+1), respectively.

On the other hand, for product-wise construction, UNIT-PREP circuit is designed to generate the following state:

𝚄𝙽𝙸𝚃-𝙿𝚁𝙴𝙿|0⟩↦∑px,py∑α∈{X,Y,Z}J1λ​|px,py⟩​|px+1,py⟩​|α⟩+J1λ​|px,py⟩​|px,py+1⟩​|α⟩+J2λ​|px,py⟩​|px+1,py+1⟩​|α⟩+J2λ​|px,py⟩​|px−1,py+1⟩​|α⟩,\displaystyle\begin{split}{\tt UNIT}\text{-}{\tt PREP}\ket{0}\mapsto\sum_{p_{x},p_{y}}\sum_{\alpha\in\{X,Y,Z\}}&\sqrt{\frac{J_{1}}{\lambda}}\ket{p_{x},p_{y}}\ket{p_{x}+1,p_{y}}\ket{\alpha}\\ +&\sqrt{\frac{J_{1}}{\lambda}}\ket{p_{x},p_{y}}\ket{p_{x},p_{y}+1}\ket{\alpha}\\ +&\sqrt{\frac{J_{2}}{\lambda}}\ket{p_{x},p_{y}}\ket{p_{x}+1,p_{y}+1}\ket{\alpha}\\ +&\sqrt{\frac{J_{2}}{\lambda}}\ket{p_{x},p_{y}}\ket{p_{x}-1,p_{y}+1}\ket{\alpha},\end{split} (S66)

whose graphical description is shown in Fig. S16(b). Note that, the required number of ancillary qubits is 3​log⁡N+O⁡(1)3\log N+O(1) rather than 2​log⁡N+O⁡(1)2\log N+O(1) that is obtained by simply adding up the numbers in Fig. S16(b). This is because the most efficient implementation of adders (in terms of TT-count) require as many quantum registers as the number of qubits to be simulated [98]. Furthermore, by counting the number of required TT-gates using the table presented in Sec. S6, we find that the UNIT-PREP can be implemented with TT-count of 20​log⁡N+48​log⁡(1/δSS)20\log N+48\log(1/\delta_{\rm SS}).

As for the SELECT oracle, we follow the framework presented in Sec. 2 for sequential construction. Meanwhile, if we use the product-wise SELECT oracle, the operation on computational bases that are not included in the signal state also becomes nontrivial, while this does not affect the dynamics encoded in the signal state. In this case, the TT-count becomes 24​N−424N-4, which is approximately halved compared to the vanilla sequential type of SELECT oracle.

2 2d Fermi-Hubbard model

The Hamiltonian of Fermi-Hubbard model on the square lattice reads as defined in Sec. S1 as

H=−t∑⟨p,q⟩,s(cp,s†cq,s+h.c.)+U∑pnp,↑np,↓,\displaystyle H=-t\sum_{\langle p,q\rangle,s}(c_{p,s}^{\dagger}c_{q,s}+{\rm h.c.})+U\sum_{p}n_{p,\uparrow}n_{p,\downarrow}, (S67)

where cp,σ(†)c_{p,\sigma}^{({\dagger})} is the fermionic annihilation (creation) operator on site pp with spin σ∈{↑,↓}\sigma\in\{\uparrow,\downarrow\}, np,σ=cp,σ†​cp,σn_{p,\sigma}=c_{p,\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{p,\sigma} is the corresponding number operator, tt is the hopping amplitude, and UU is the repulsive onsite potential. As in the case for spin-1/2 J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model, we mainly consider the lattice of M×MM\times M sites, and thus the total number of qubits required to simulate the system is N=2​M2N=2M^{2}. While we take tt to be unity in this work, we explicitly keep it among expressions when it is more informative.

For concreteness, we assume to employ the Jordan-Wigner transformation to encode fermionic degrees of freedom into quantum computer:

cp,s(†)=sgn⁡(s)​∏r<p∏s=↑,↓σr,s+(−)\displaystyle c_{p,s}^{({\dagger})}={\rm sgn}(s)\prod_{r<p}\prod_{s=\uparrow,\downarrow}\sigma_{r,s}^{+(-)} (S68)

where p=px+py​Mp=p_{x}+p_{y}M and sgn⁡(s){\rm sgn}(s) takes ±1\pm 1 according to whether the spin is up or down. This leads us to the expression of Hamiltonian as follows,

H=−t2∑⟨p,q⟩,s(σp,sXσZ→σq,sX+σp,sYσZ→σq,sY)+U4∑pσp,↑Zσp,↓Z−U4∑p,sσp,sZ+U​N8I,\displaystyle H=-\frac{t}{2}\sum_{\langle p,q\rangle,s}(\sigma_{p,s}^{X}\sigma^{\vec{Z}}\sigma_{q,s}^{X}+\sigma_{p,s}^{Y}\sigma^{\vec{Z}}\sigma_{q,s}^{Y})+\frac{U}{4}\sum_{p}\sigma^{Z}_{p,\uparrow}\sigma^{Z}_{p,\downarrow}-\frac{U}{4}\sum_{p,s}\sigma_{p,s}^{Z}+\frac{UN}{8}I, (S69)

where we have introduced σZ→\sigma^{\vec{Z}} to represent the Z-string generated by Jordan-Wigner transformation. While one may use this definition, we may also employ an alternative definition with shift in the potential term as ∑pnp,↑​np,↓→∑pnp,↑​np,↓−U2​∑p,snp,s+U4​I\sum_{p}n_{p,\uparrow}n_{p,\downarrow}\rightarrow\sum_{p}n_{p,\uparrow}n_{p,\downarrow}-\frac{U}{2}\sum_{p,s}n_{p,s}+\frac{U}{4}I, which results in the simplified form as

H=−t2∑⟨p,q⟩(σp,sXσZ→σq,sX+σp,sYσZ→σq,sY)+U4∑pσp,↑Zσp,↓Z.\displaystyle H=-\frac{t}{2}\sum_{\langle p,q\rangle}(\sigma_{p,s}^{X}\sigma^{\vec{Z}}\sigma_{q,s}^{X}+\sigma_{p,s}^{Y}\sigma^{\vec{Z}}\sigma_{q,s}^{Y})+\frac{U}{4}\sum_{p}\sigma_{p,\uparrow}^{Z}\sigma_{p,\downarrow}^{Z}. (S70)

While this shift does not significantly change the TT-count of oracles, it slightly modifies the L1 norm of the Hamiltonian which affects the total gate count, as discussed below.

In similar to the case with 2d J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model, we first introduce the sequential construction of UNIT-PREP. Our construction simply aims to generate

𝚄𝙽𝙸𝚃​-​𝙿𝚁𝙴𝙿​|0⟩↦∑px,py[U4​λ|p,↑⟩|onsite interaction⟩α,μ+∑s=↑,↓∑μ=ex,ey,e−x,e−yt2​λ|p,s⟩|hopping towards ​μ⟩α,μ],\displaystyle\begin{split}{\tt UNIT}\text{-}{\tt PREP}\ket{0}\mapsto&\sum_{p_{x},p_{y}}\Bigg[\sqrt{\frac{U}{4\lambda}}\ket{p,\uparrow}\ket{\text{onsite interaction}}_{\alpha,\mu}\\ +&\sum_{s=\uparrow,\downarrow}\sum_{\mu=e_{x},e_{y},e_{-x},e_{-y}}\sqrt{\frac{t}{2\lambda}}\ket{p,s}\ket{\text{hopping towards }\mu}_{\alpha,\mu}\Bigg],\end{split} (S71)

which is realized by circuit shown in Fig. S17(a). Note that the ancillary quantum states such as |onsite interaction⟩\ket{\text{onsite~interaction}} functions as “flag” to tell the SELECT oracle which interaction term must be operated. Here, the L1 norm is explicitly given as λ=λt+λU\lambda=\lambda_{t}+\lambda_{U} where the contribution from the hopping term is λt=t⋅(#​edges)\lambda_{t}=t\cdot{\rm(\#edges)} and that from the interaction term is λU=18​U​N\lambda_{U}=\frac{1}{8}UN. We comment that this value is slightly different from λU=12​U​N\lambda_{U}=\frac{1}{2}UN as employed in Ref. [92], which takes the constant term into account. However, the constant term can be eliminated from the QPE algorithm since we do not need to estimate its value. This results in a slightly smaller λ\lambda so that the repetition count of SELECT oracle is suppressed.

By carefully examining the coefficients and the commutation relation, we find out that UNIT-PREP presented in Fig. S17(b) provides the the product-wise construction via the following operation:

𝚄𝙽𝙸𝚃​-​𝙿𝚁𝙴𝙿​|0⟩↦∑px,py[U4​λ|px,py,↑⟩|px,py,↓⟩|1⟩α+∑s=↑,↓t2​λ​(|px,py,s⟩​|px+1,py,s⟩​|0⟩α+|px,py,s⟩​|px,py+1,s⟩​|0⟩α)+∑s=↑,↓t2​λ(|px,py,s⟩|px−1,py,s⟩|0⟩α+|px,py,s⟩|px,py−1,s⟩|0⟩α)],\displaystyle\begin{split}{\tt UNIT}\text{-}{\tt PREP}\ket{0}\mapsto&\sum_{p_{x},p_{y}}\Bigg[\sqrt{\frac{U}{4\lambda}}\ket{p_{x},p_{y},\uparrow}\ket{p_{x},p_{y},\downarrow}\ket{1}_{\alpha}\\ +&\sum_{s=\uparrow,\downarrow}\sqrt{\frac{t}{2\lambda}}\Bigl(\ket{p_{x},p_{y},s}\ket{p_{x}+1,p_{y},s}\ket{0}_{\alpha}+\ket{p_{x},p_{y},s}\ket{p_{x},p_{y}+1,s}\ket{0}_{\alpha}\Bigr)\\ +&\sum_{s=\uparrow,\downarrow}\sqrt{\frac{t}{2\lambda}}\Bigl(\ket{p_{x},p_{y},s}\ket{p_{x}-1,p_{y},s}\ket{0}_{\alpha}+\ket{p_{x},p_{y},s}\ket{p_{x},p_{y}-1,s}\ket{0}_{\alpha}\Bigr)\Bigg],\end{split} (S72)

where α\alpha specifies the type of interaction term.

Now we proceed to the operation of SELECT. We remark that the sequential construction is straightforward, and can be done by following the procedure explained as in Fig. S15(a). In contrast, the product-wise construction of SELECT is rather nontrivial; given a signal state as presented in Eq. (S72), the operation of SELECT shall satisfy

𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃​|px,py,s𝐩,qx,qy,s𝐪,α⟩​|ψ⟩\displaystyle{\tt SELECT}\ket{p_{x},p_{y},s_{\bf p},q_{x},q_{y},s_{\bf q},\alpha}\ket{\psi} (S73)
=\displaystyle= |px,py,s𝐩,qx,qy,s𝐪,α⟩⊗{σp,↑Z​σq,↓Z​|ψ⟩if p=q,(sp,sq)=(↑,↓),α=1σp,spX​(∏p<r<q,srσr,srZ)​σq,sqX​|ψ⟩if ​p<q,sp=sq,|𝐩−𝐪|=1,α=0σq,sqY​(∏q<r<p,srσr,srZ)​σp,spY​|ψ⟩if ​q<p,sp=sq,|𝐩−𝐪|=1,α=0\displaystyle\ket{p_{x},p_{y},s_{\bf p},q_{x},q_{y},s_{\bf q},\alpha}\otimes\begin{cases}\sigma_{p,\uparrow}^{Z}\sigma_{q,\downarrow}^{Z}\ket{\psi}&\text{if~}p=q,(s_{p},s_{q})=(\uparrow,\downarrow),\alpha=1\\ \sigma_{p,s_{p}}^{X}(\prod_{p<r<q,s_{r}}\sigma_{r,s_{r}}^{Z})\sigma_{q,s_{q}}^{X}\ket{\psi}&\text{if~}p<q,s_{p}=s_{q},|{\bf p}-{\bf q}|=1,\alpha=0\\ \sigma_{q,s_{q}}^{Y}(\prod_{q<r<p,s_{r}}\sigma_{r,s_{r}}^{Z})\sigma_{p,s_{p}}^{Y}\ket{\psi}&\text{if~}q<p,s_{p}=s_{q},|{\bf p}-{\bf q}|=1,\alpha=0\end{cases} (S74)

where the operation on subspace outside the signal state is unrestricted as long as 𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃2=I{\tt SELECT}^{2}=I is satisfied. Note that comparison between pp and qq is based on the integer p=px+py​Mp=p_{x}+p_{y}M and q=qx+qy​Mq=q_{x}+q_{y}M while ‖𝐩−𝐪‖\|{\bf p}-{\bf q}\| denotes the Manhattan distance on the square lattice. Product-wise construction of SELECT oracle for the Fermi-Hubbard model has been suggested by Babbush et al., which pointed out that the construction can be done by structure shown in Fig. S18 with TT-count of 10​N10N [92], as opposed to the one by the sequential type of 18​N18N. Note that, the TT-count of sequential type without shifting the potential term is 22​N22N.

3 Spin-1 antiferromagnetic Heisenberg chain

Recall that the Hamiltonian of spin-1 antiferromagnetic Heisenberg chain reads

H=∑p=1Nsite∑α∈{X,Y,Z}Spα​Sp+1α,\displaystyle H=\sum_{p=1}^{N_{\rm site}}\sum_{\alpha\in\{X,Y,Z\}}S_{p}^{\alpha}S_{p+1}^{\alpha}, (S75)

where SpαS_{p}^{\alpha} is the spin-1 operator acting on the pp-th site and NsiteN_{\rm site} denotes the number of sites in the system. To render the problem compatible with quantum computers that take qubits as a elementary unit of quantum registers, we shall encode the system into enlarged Hilbert space spanned solely by qubits. In this regard, we represent each spin operator SpαS_{p}^{\alpha} as a sum of Pauli operators as Spα=12​∑ν=12​Sσp,ναS_{p}^{\alpha}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\nu=1}^{2S}\sigma_{p,\nu}^{\alpha} and rewrite the Hamiltonian as

H=14​∑p=1Nsite∑ν,τ=12​S∑α∈{X,Y,Z}σp,να​σp+1,τα.\displaystyle H=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{p=1}^{N_{\rm site}}\sum_{\nu,\tau=1}^{2S}\sum_{\alpha\in\{X,Y,Z\}}\sigma_{p,\nu}^{\alpha}\sigma_{p+1,\tau}^{\alpha}. (S76)

Note that we also assume that the trial state for quantum phase estimation is also represented using the qubit encoding.

From the expression of Hamiltonian, we deduce that the UNIT-PREP circuit under periodic boundary condition can be composed as shown in Fig. S19 to generate the following state:

𝚄𝙽𝙸𝚃​-​𝙿𝚁𝙴𝙿​|0⟩log⁡Nsite+2↦∑p,α∈{X,Y,Z}1λ​|p⟩​|α⟩.\displaystyle{\tt UNIT}\text{-}{\tt PREP}\ket{0}^{\log N_{\rm site}+2}\mapsto\sum_{p,\alpha\in\{X,Y,Z\}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda}}\ket{p}\ket{\alpha}. (S77)

Correspondingly, the SELECT in the case of qubitization is constructed following the one presented in Fig. S15(a) such that

𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃​|p,α,ν,τ⟩​|ψ⟩=|p,α,ν,τ⟩​σp,να​σp+1,τα​|ψ⟩,\displaystyle{\tt SELECT}\ket{p,\alpha,\nu,\tau}\ket{\psi}=\ket{p,\alpha,\nu,\tau}\sigma_{p,\nu}^{\alpha}\sigma_{p+1,\tau}^{\alpha}\ket{\psi}, (S78)

which can be realized by the general sequential implementation of  SELECT by TT-count of 48​S2​Nsite−448S^{2}N_{\rm site}-4. One may alternatively consider the product-wise implementation of SELECT as in Fig. S15(b) by consuming TT-count of 48​S​Nsite−448SN_{\rm site}-4. However, we point out that there is no advantage in terms of TT-count for S=1S=1 case, while it requires additional log⁡Nsite\log N_{\rm site} ancillary qubits. Therefore, we perform our runtime estimation based on the former implementation.

S6 Complexity of basic quantum operations

Here we provide the details on the basic quantum operations that are used for circuit construction and TT-count analysis.

One of the most important operation that are commonly used in various basic gates presented in Table S9 is the logical AND operation, whose explicit Clifford+TT construction is provided in Fig. S20(a). Gidney showed that, by consuming ancillary qubits to store the temporal results of addition, we can implement nn-qubit logical adder with TT-count of 4​n+O⁡(1)4n+O(1) and controlled adder with 8​n+O⁡(1)8n+O(1) [98] (Fig. S20(b)). We further push the use of temporary ancilla qubit to reduce the TT-count for other controlled operations, such as mm-controlled addition, SWAP, or rotation (See Fig. S20(c), (d)). Also, we implement the UNIFORM operation following the construction scheme presented in Ref. [92]. Finally, as a variant of the adder, we introduce a constant adder that performs some constant binary addition as shown in Figs. S21.

S7 Szegedy quantum walk with imperfect PREPARE

In Sec. 4, we have seen that the Szegedy-type quantum walk operator enables us to explore the energy spectra of the block-encoded Hermitian operator. In particular, the oracular unitaries can be implemented efficiently if the Hamiltonian exhibit spatially periodic structure with N𝜶=O⁡(1)N_{\bm{\alpha}}=O(1) types of interaction coefficients. However, this argument strongly depends on the boundary condition; when the model is defined with open boundary condition or cylindrical boundary condition, the interaction configurations differ at the boundary sites, which affects the complexity of the PREPARE oracle in particular. Although the TT-gate complexity of PREPARE remains to be log⁡(N/ϵ)\log(N/\epsilon) and therefore does not dominate the total cost even when we incorporate boundary effect, it is desirable to deal with minimal effort.

Here, we present a method that use homogeneous implementation of PREPARE and still extract simulation results for lattice systems defined under boundary conditions that are not necessarily periodic along all directions. To be concrete, we find that the error in the operation can be readily absorbed by constant shift in the Hamiltonian.

Let us first consider a perfect and also a slightly erroneous PREPARE operation that takes the ancillary system to the following states:

𝙿𝚁𝙴𝙿𝙰𝚁𝙴0:|0⟩⊗a↦|ℒ0⟩\displaystyle{\tt PREPARE}_{0}:\ket{0}^{\otimes a}\mapsto\ket{\mathcal{L}_{0}} =\displaystyle= ∑l=1Lwlλ​|l⟩,\displaystyle\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sqrt{\frac{w_{l}}{\lambda}}\ket{l}, (S79)
𝙿𝚁𝙴𝙿𝙰𝚁𝙴:|0⟩⊗a↦|ℒ⟩\displaystyle{\tt PREPARE}:\ket{0}^{\otimes a}\mapsto\ket{\mathcal{L}} =\displaystyle= β1​|ℒ0⟩+β2​|⟂⟩,\displaystyle\beta_{1}\ket{\mathcal{L}_{0}}+\beta_{2}\ket{\perp}, (S80)

where |⟂⟩\ket{\perp} is orthogonal to any |l⟩.\ket{l}. Our goal is to perform unbiased simulation of Szegedy quantum walk so that the obtained results correctly extracts the eigenspectra of the Hamiltonian. One naive solution is to “correct” the state from |ℒ0⟩\ket{\mathcal{L}_{0}} to |ℒ⟩\ket{\mathcal{L}} via, e.g., amplitude amplification. Meanwhile, by making use of the specific structure of SELECT considered in this work, we can eliminate the error with negligible cost. To be specific, we assume that the SELECT operates nontrivially only in the subspace Π​ℋ​Π\Pi\mathcal{H}\Pi where Π=(∑l=1LI⊗n⊗|l⟩​⟨l|)\Pi=(\sum_{l=1}^{L}I^{\otimes n}\otimes\ket{l}\bra{l}) and ℋ\mathcal{H} is the total Hilbert space (confirm that this is satisfied in our construction presented in Sec. 4.). Under such an assumption, we introduce a constant shift γ\gamma to the Hamiltonian to absorb the error. The overlaps are explicitly written as

(⟨ℒ0|⊗I)​𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃​(|ℒ0⟩⊗I)\displaystyle(\bra{\mathcal{L}_{0}}\otimes I){\tt SELECT}(\ket{\mathcal{L}_{0}}\otimes I) =\displaystyle= H0λ+γ⁡(−I),\displaystyle\frac{H_{0}}{\lambda}+\gamma(-I), (S81)
(⟨⟂|⊗I)​𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃​(|⟂⟩⊗I)\displaystyle(\bra{\perp}\otimes I){\tt SELECT}(\ket{\perp}\otimes I) =\displaystyle= I,\displaystyle I, (S82)
(⟨⟂|⊗I)​𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃​(|ℒ0⟩⊗I)\displaystyle(\bra{\perp}\otimes I){\tt SELECT}(\ket{\mathcal{L}_{0}}\otimes I) =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0, (S83)

which leads to

(⟨ℒ|⊗I)​𝚂𝙴𝙻𝙴𝙲𝚃​(|ℒ⟩⊗I)=|β1|2​H0λ+(−γ​|β1|2+|β2|2)​I.\displaystyle(\bra{\mathcal{L}}\otimes I){\tt SELECT}(\ket{\mathcal{L}}\otimes I)=\frac{|\beta_{1}|^{2}H_{0}}{\lambda}+(-\gamma|\beta_{1}|^{2}+|\beta_{2}|^{2})I. (S84)

Therefore, if we pick γ=|β2|2/|β1|2\gamma=|\beta_{2}|^{2}/|\beta_{1}|^{2}, we can simulate the rescaled version of Hamiltonian.

For concreteness, let us consider a case where we want to simulate a lattice system with cylindrical boundary condition using PREPARE that is intended for periodic boundary condition. We argue that the overhead due to the rescaling is negligible. This can be understood from the fact that the TT-count for estimating the eigenenergy (at arbitrary precision) using the Taylorization or qubitization algorithm is proportional to λ\lambda. As can be seen from Eq. (S84), the L1 norm of the coefficient is amplified under the erroneous signal state |ℒ⟩\ket{\mathcal{L}} as λ→λ/|β1|2\lambda\rightarrow\lambda/|\beta_{1}|^{2}. Since the ratio of coefficients is given as |β2/β1|2=O((Nd−1d/N)2)=O(N−2/d)|\beta_{2}/\beta_{1}|^{2}=O((N^{\frac{d-1}{d}}/N)^{2})=O(N^{-2/d}) in dd-dimensional lattice systems with local interactions, we straightforwardly obtain |β1|2≈1|\beta_{1}|^{2}\approx 1, and thus does not affect the overall cost up to the leading order. Throughout this work, for TT-count and runtime analysis we assume to employ PREPARE oracle designed to implement a signal state for periodic boundary condition.

S8 Runtime analysis of qubitization-based quantum phase estimation

1 Overview

In this section, we explain the details of the runtime analysis for the quantum phase estimation that is based on the qubitization algorithm. As we have shortly mentioned in Sec. 4, the runtime of quantum circuits represented with the Clifford+TT formalism is typically evaluated with the number of TT-gates, known as TT-count, in the compiled quantum circuits. This is because each application of TT-gates requires a time-consuming procedure consisting of magic-state injection, distillation, and teleportation in typical quantum error-correcting codes stabilized by Pauli operators. This is why we have compared the Hamiltonian simulation subroutines in Table  1 in the main text. While the TT-count can capture the time-scaling of quantum algorithms when magic-state preparations are the most time-consuming factors, this estimation loses several vital factors in time analysis, and the actual execution time can vary a few orders of magnitudes depending on the strategy of compilation and executions. Here, we review several standard strategies and show how we calculated the execution times.

Throughout this paper, we assume the following situations: 1) Physical qubits are allocated on the vertices of 2d grids, which we call a qubit plane. 2) Logical qubits are encoded with surface codes [101, 102, 103, 104]. 3) Logical operations are constructed based on twist-based lattice surgery [105, 103]. 4) The method introduced by Litinski [106] is applied to the construction of magic-state distillation, and purpose-specific strategies are employed for the compilation of SELECT and PREPARE oracles. Note that these assumptions may change or become unnecessary in the future by using devices with more flexible connectivity or employing other logical-operation strategies such as defect-pair braiding [104] and twist-free approach [107]. Nevertheless, we focus on the above scenario since they are standard assumptions in relevant studies on the runtime analysis [108, 12], and we leave the other scenario as future work.

2 Surface code and lattice surgery

In fault-tolerant quantum computing with surface codes, each logical qubit is allocated as a d×dd\times d block on the qubit plane, where dd is the distance of surface codes. The error rates of logical qubits decrease exponentially with respect to dd, as far as the error rates of physical qubits are smaller than the value called threshold. The required dd is determined from physical error rates of given devices, logical-error suppression rate in error-correcting codes, and required logical error rates. During the computation, we repeat a set of Pauli measurements called stabilizer measurements, according to the generator set of a stabilizer group. A period for all the stabilizer Pauli measurements is called a code cycle. The recovery Pauli operations are estimated with a delay due to classical processing and stored in the unit logic called Pauli frame [103, 109].

All the basic logical operations must be achieved fault-tolerantly. The lattice surgery [105] is known to be the most promising strategy to efficiently achieve multi-qubit logical operations in fault-tolerant quantum computing. In this strategy, the logical Pauli measurements on multiple logical qubits are realized by connecting corresponding blocks with a proper circumference, and all the logical Clifford operations are performed via the logical measurements using lattice surgery and logical HH and SS gates. The time required for the multi-qubit logical Pauli measurements with the lattice surgery is independent of the number of the target logical qubits but linearly scales to the code distance dd. Thus, it is convenient to define another unit, code beat, as the latency of dd code cycles. We need 22 code beats for logical SS and CNOT gates and 33 code beats for logical HH gates. Thanks to the nature of CSS codes, the latency for destructive single-qubit Pauli-X,ZX,Z measurements and the preparation of the logical eigenstate of Pauli-X,ZX,Z are finished within a single code cycle. Since we can take their latency into account by increasing the code beat, we neglect their latency hereafter. Since lattice-surgery operations require ancillary logical-qubit cells that connect target logical qubits, the throughput of lattice-surgery operations depends on topological restrictions such as the allocation of logical qubits and routing of ancillary-qubit paths. See Ref. [105, 103, 108] for the detailed rules of the lattice surgery.

The non-Clifford gates, such as TT and Toffoli gates, cannot be performed with the combinations of the Clifford operations, and are known to take a longer time compared with the other operations. These operations are achieved with the gate-teleportation technique that consumes quantum resources named the magic states. For instance, when one desires to operate a TT-gate through its teleportation, we need a logical qubit prepared in a magic state |A⟩=1/2​(|0⟩+ei​π/4​|1⟩)\ket{A}=1/\sqrt{2}(\ket{0}+e^{i\pi/4}\ket{1}). While the noisy preparation of magic states can be achieved with the magic-state injection protocol, its infidelity is unacceptable for fault-tolerant operations. Therefore, we must create a magic state from a protocol called magic-state distillation, which allows the generation of magic states with arbitrarily small infidelity. A standard magic-state distillation protocol is 15-to-1 distillation. This protocol creates a single clean magic state from 15 noisy magic states to reduce the infidelity of magic states from pp to 35​p335p^{3}, and succeeds with probability 1−15​p1-15p [103]. The latency of a single trial of magic-state injection requires constant code cycles. Typically, we need two-level distillation for the required logical error rate, and each generation requires 1515 code beats with the construction proposed in Ref. [106]. Note that large code distances are not required at the first distillation level since we only need to protect noisy magic states during distillation. Thus, the latency may be smaller. We typically assign a region of the qubit plane just for repeating magic-state preparation, which we call a magic-state factory. The teleportation of non-Clifford gates requires the feedback of a Clifford operation or the adaptive change of consequent Pauli measurement basis. Thus, successive gate teleportation will be blocked for a period of error-estimation delay, which is called a reaction time. The reaction time is determined by the throughput of the error-estimation algorithm for surface codes, physical error rates, chosen code distances, and its circuit implementation. It should be noted that, unlike Clifford operations, the most time-consuming part of non-Clifford gates is the magic-state preparation. This process can be performed in advance, and the preparation part can always be parallelized by assigning many magic-state factories. This makes basic optimization methods and bottleneck analysis for Clifford and non-Clifford gates different.

3 Time estimation without topological restriction

The runtime estimation of quantum algorithms is a key part of resource estimation and finding the crossover point of quantum advantage. In this section, we explain methods to estimate the runtime of quantum programs that are written in terms of Clifford+TT formulation. As we detail below, the appropriate runtime estimation heavily relies on the hardware configuration and compilation settings. To estimate actual runtime with reasonable costs, there are two runtime-estimation strategies. One is heuristically estimating the runtime from several critical parameters such as TT-count and depth, and the other is calculating the runtime with software simulation of fault-tolerant quantum computers. In the following, we introduce the first strategy in two different situations, the TT-count limited and reaction limited estimations, as ones of the most commonly employed estimation strategies. We subsequently point out their defects and explain how to overcome them by software simulation while explicitly considering the topological restriction of logical qubits.

If quantum circuits consume magic states with a constant rate, we can roughly estimate the execution time by counting the number of TT-gate. On the other hand, the consumption rate of magic states is not necessarily constant and the execution time may not be linear to the number of TT-gates. Fortunately, there is a canonical form proposed by Litinski [106] that ensures an almost constant consumption rate of magic states. In this formalism, we convert the Clifford+TT circuits to two stacks of layers; the first one is a sequence of π/8\pi/8 Pauli rotations, and the latter is a sequence of Pauli measurements. The number of π/8\pi/8 Pauli rotations is equal to the number of TT-gates NTN_{T}. The execution of π/8\pi/8 Pauli rotation consumes a single magic state, and is achieved with a single code beat and post-processing on the ancillary qubits. Based on Litinski’s formalism, the estimation of the execution time with the Clifford+TT formalism in a qubit-restricted situation is simple. Assuming that we have a small qubit plane and the number of the magic-state factory is very restricted, we can expect that the latter Pauli measurement part is negligible compared to the first π/8\pi/8 rotation parts. Thus, the execution time can be estimated as the τT​NT\tau_{T}N_{T}, where τT\tau_{T} is the average time for generating a magic state and teleporting it. This is called a TT-count limited estimation. In the most pessimistic scenario, we can only place a single factory on the qubit plane and the consumption rate of TT-gate is much more frequent than the generation rate of a magic state factory. In this case, the execution time of quantum phase estimation can be obtained by multiplying the number of TT-gates for SELECT and PREPARE oracles.

We can also consider the opposite scenario; we have a large qubit plane and can create arbitrary many magic-state factories. In this case, we can effectively have an on-demand magic-state supply. Thus, we can teleport multiple TT-gates as far as they can be executed in parallel. Therefore, we assume that each simultaneous application is achieved with τgroup=min⁡(τtel,τreact)\tau_{\rm group}={\rm min}(\tau_{\rm tel},\tau_{\rm react}), where τtel\tau_{\rm tel} is the latency of lattice-surgery operations for the magic-state teleportation and τreact\tau_{\rm react} is the reaction time. This quantity is directly related with the execution time as DT​τgroupD_{T}\tau_{\rm group}, where DTD_{T} is the number of TT-depth. When τtel>τreact\tau_{\rm tel}>\tau_{\rm react}, we can hide the latency τtel\tau_{\rm tel} by time-optimal construction [110, 106]. With ancillary qubits, we can convert the iterations of gate teleportation to parallel teleportation and a sequence of reactions. When we can utilize KK times larger qubit space, we can force τgroup∼DT​τtel/K+DT​τreact\tau_{\rm group}\sim D_{T}\tau_{\rm tel}/K+D_{T}\tau_{\rm react}. This situation is called a reaction-limited. An actual scenario would be the intermediate of the above two, and the actual execution time varies according to the size of the available qubit plane size.

In the above strategy, the TT-count and depth of SELECT and PREPARE oracles are critical parameters. In the case of the ground-state energy estimation for condensed matter Hamiltonians, the coefficients of Hamiltonians are nearly uniform, and therefore the execution time is expected to be dominated by SELECT modules (See Sec. 4). To implement SELECT operation with a small number of TT-gates, we use a method proposed in Ref. [92]. The action of SELECT operations defined in Eq. (S58) is divided into the product of small commutative unitary operations ∏l=0L−1Ul\prod_{l=0}^{L-1}U_{l} where Ul=|l⟩​⟨l|⊗Hl+(I−|l⟩​⟨l|)⊗IU_{l}=\ket{l}\bra{l}\otimes H_{l}+(I-\ket{l}\bra{l})\otimes I. To construct UlU_{l}, i.e., a gate controlled by ⌈log⁡L⌉\lceil\log L\rceil-qubit input register |l⟩\ket{l}, we use (⌈log⁡L⌉−1)(\lceil\log L\rceil-1) ancillary qubits and map |x⟩​|ψ⟩​|0⟩\ket{x}\ket{\psi}\ket{0} to |x⟩​|ψ⟩​|cx,l⟩\ket{x}\ket{\psi}\ket{c_{x,l}}, where cx,l∈{0,1}(⌈log⁡L⌉−1)c_{x,l}\in\{0,1\}^{(\lceil\log L\rceil-1)} and the last bit of cx,lc_{x,l} is 11 if x=lx=l and 0 if x≠lx\neq l. Then, we can achieve an action |x⟩​|ψ⟩​|cx,l⟩↦(Ul​|x⟩​|ψ⟩)​|cx,l⟩=|x⟩⁡(Hl′​|ψ⟩)​|cx,l⟩\ket{x}\ket{\psi}\ket{c_{x,l}}\mapsto(U_{l}\ket{x}\ket{\psi})\ket{c_{x,l}}=\ket{x}(H_{l}^{\prime}\ket{\psi})\ket{c_{x,l}} where Hl′=HlH_{l}^{\prime}=H_{l} if l=xl=x and Hl=IH_{l}=I otherwise, using a Clifford operation |0⟩​⟨0|⊗I+|1⟩​⟨1|⊗Hl\ket{0}\bra{0}\otimes I+\ket{1}\bra{1}\otimes H_{l} where the control qubit corresponds to the last qubit of |cx,l⟩\ket{c_{x,l}}. To discuss the placement of logical qubits in the next subsection, we denote the register |x⟩\ket{x} and |cx,l⟩\ket{c_{x,l}} as control qubits, and |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} as system qubits. Also, we denote the last qubit of |cx,l⟩\ket{c_{x,l}} as tail control qubit since among the control qubits, only the tail control qubit interacts with system qubits in this iteration. The quantum circuit based on this iteration is shown in Fig. S22 (a). At the first iteration, we construct |x⟩​|0⟩↦|x⟩​|cx,0⟩\ket{x}\ket{0}\mapsto\ket{x}\ket{c_{x,0}}, of which the action is shown as Initialize. In the ii-th iteration, we need to update the state as |x⟩​|cx,i⟩↦|x⟩​|cx,i+1⟩\ket{x}\ket{c_{x,i}}\mapsto\ket{x}\ket{c_{x,i+1}}, which is achieved by a unitary operation named Uinc,iU_{{\rm inc},i}. Finally, the ancillary qubits are disentangled as |x⟩​|cx,L−1⟩↦|x⟩​|0⟩\ket{x}\ket{c_{x,L-1}}\mapsto\ket{x}\ket{0} with Finalize. This method enables the implementation of SELECT operations with TT-count of 4​L−44L-4.

The above construction of SELECT operation is a serial sequence of Toffoli gates for Initialize, Uinc,iU_{{\rm inc},i}, and Finalize. Thus, its TT-depth is almost equal to TT-count. This means there is no room to reduce TT-depth even when several magic-state factories are available. To enable a flexible performance tuning of SELECT operations according to available magic-state supply rates, we propose a technique to reduce the TT-depth with a similar idea of loop-parallelization in classical computing (See Fig. S22 (b)). Suppose that the target Hamiltonian consists of LL terms of Pauli operators acting on nn qubits. In this technique, we divide the task of SELECT operations to bb parallelized executions using bb times the number of control qubits as follows. First, we clone the input control registers to GHZ states ∑xαx​|x⟩↦∑xαx​|x⟩⊗b\sum_{x}\alpha_{x}\ket{x}\mapsto\sum_{x}\alpha_{x}\ket{x}^{\otimes b}, which is denoted as CopyIndex operation, and we call each cloned control register as a thread. Then, we divide the LL terms to bb blocks, where the ii-th block contains terms indexed from (i​L/b)(iL/b) to ((i+1)​L/b−1)((i+1)L/b-1), and SELECT operations is performed as bb independent iterations by bb threads. Finally, we uncompute the cloned registers. This construction effectively reduces the TT-depth from O⁡(L)O(L) to O⁡(L/b+log⁡L)O(L/b+\log L) with an additional O⁡(b​log⁡n)O(b\log n) qubits. The brief construction of this parallelization is shown in Fig. S22 (b). Note that as far as we keep bb sufficiently small than nn, the overhead of O⁡(b​log⁡n)O(b\log n) ancillary qubits would be negligible compared to the system size nn. The detailed decomposition and parallelization efficiency will be presented in another paper.

Although the TT-count limited or reaction limited estimation based on the above counting provides a rough estimation of runtime, it should be noted that they ignore the overhead by topological restriction of the qubit plane. Since each logical qubit is placed at a certain position on the qubit plane and we need to connect the target blocks for lattice surgery, we sometimes cannot execute operations due to the conflict of their paths. This means TT-gates are not necessarily teleported in parallel even if they are located in parallel on the quantum circuit representation. To take them into account, we need to consider the allocation of logical qubits and their routing for lattice-surgery operations, which is discussed in the next section.

4 Placement of logical qubits and routing for lattice surgery

Once quantum circuits are translated to the sequence of intrinsic lattice-surgery operations, we need to place each logical qubit to a certain block on the qubit plane. While we should choose dense allocations to avoid the redundant usage of the qubit plane, too dense allocations may lead to path conflicts and the degradation of instruction throughput. In this paper, we heuristically designed the placement of logical qubits for condensed matter Hamiltonians for 2d spins by leveraging the feature of spatially local interactions. Our logical qubits mapping and correspondence to SELECT circuits is illustrated in Fig. S23.

In our design, the qubit plane is divided into three parts; factory, control, and system. We assume that the design of magic state factories proposed by Litinski [106] is used and they are simply located in the factory parts. So, we explain the detailed logical-qubit placement of the system and control parts. The system part is used for locating system qubits in SELECT operation. For the 2d Heisenberg models, the position of system qubits representing a spin at a certain coordinate is placed at the same coordinate of the system part to leverage the locality. For the 2d Fermi-Hubbard models, we heuristically determined the positions of system qubits according to those of fermions. Since Clifford operations and lattice surgery need ancillary space around the logical-qubit cells, we created O⁡(n)O(\sqrt{n}) corridors of ancillary space so that the vertical and horizontal edges of each logical-qubit cell touch them. Note that this is one of the most compact allocations while keeping Clifford operations available [107, 103]. We use this compact allocation for the system part because of the observation that system qubits are less frequently accessed compared to the control part, and the compact allocation of the system part reduces the required number of physical qubits without losing the parallelism of SELECT operations.

The control part is used for locating control qubits in SELECT operations, i.e., input register |x⟩\ket{x} and ancillary register |cx,l⟩\ket{c_{x,l}}. Since the operations on this part are dominated by Toffoli-gates acting on the neighboring bits in the registers, we placed logical qubits for them as arrays in the order of head bits to tail bits. An example allocation of the control part is shown in Fig. S22(c), where an array of dark cells corresponds to the input register and that of light cells to the ancillary register.

After we determine the placement for each part, we need to map the location of the three parts on the qubit plane. As shown in Fig. S23, we allocate three parts in the order of factory, control, and system parts. The factory part is placed behind the control part since control qubits consume magic states while system qubits do not. Also, since only the tail control qubits in the control part interact with the system part, we let the system part touch the side of the control part where the tail control qubits are located.

When we utilize the parallelization to the control part, we modify the qubit allocation of the control part as shown in Fig. S22(d). If the Pauli terms are randomly assigned to each thread, tail control qubits of the threads try to touch system qubits at random positions, which induces the conflicts of Clifford operations and may become a bottleneck. This problem can be resolved by re-ordering the Pauli terms and appropriate block allocations. Since we now consider nearly uniform coefficients, the cost of PREPARE oracle is almost independent of the ordering of coefficients. Thus, we can change the order of Pauli terms to minimize the execution time for SELECT operations. Suppose the list of sorted indices in the ii-th Pauli operator is (j1,…​jk)(j_{1},...j_{k}). Then, we sort the Pauli terms with the set in ascending order, separate them into bb blocks, and assign them to each thread. When the thread number bb satisfies n>b\sqrt{n}>b, n/b+k\sqrt{n}/b+k corridors are relevant to each thread. With this assignment, there are no potential conflicts as far as k<n/bk<\sqrt{n}/b. Thus, we can expect this assignment will prevent the potential conflict of lattice-surgery paths.

Finally, we schedule the order of instructions and determine ancillary cells for logical operations. We translate Clifford+TT formalism into a 1D sequence of SS, HH, magic-state generation, one-body Pauli measurement, and two-body lattice-surgery operations. Each instruction becomes ready for execution when all the instructions that act on the target logical qubits earlier than the target instruction. Several instructions, such as feedback operations of TT-gate teleportation, need to wait for relevant measurement outcomes to be error-corrected, i.e., there is a latency of reaction time. For logical SS and HH gates, logical qubits consume one of the neighboring and available ancillary cells. If there is no available ancillary cell, instructions wait for the next code beat. For lattice-surgery instruction, we find one of the shortest paths between target logical qubits with the breadth-first search algorithm and consume the ancillary cells on the path. If there is no path between logical qubits, instructions wait for the next code beat.

5 Parameter estimation and numerical evaluation

Here, we estimate the relevant parameters according to the recent device technologies. We define dd, LL, and mm as a code distance, the number of terms in the target Hamiltonian, and the required digit of the ground energy, respectively. They are left as variables since they depend on the problem size. While a shorter code cycle is preferable to shorten the execution time, it is lower-bounded by the time for stabilizer measurements and error estimation algorithms. Currently, the latter is the dominant factor and is expected to be no shorter than 1​μ​s1~{\rm\mu s} [111]. Thus, the code beat, which is defined by dd code cycles, is d​μ​sd~{\rm\mu s}. The time for two-level magic-state distillation τT\tau_{T} is 15​d​μ​s15d~{\rm\mu s}. The reaction time is typically assumed to be 10​μ​s10~{\rm\mu s}. The TT-count for the SELECT operation is 4​L4L and the TT-depth is 4​L/b4L/b, where bb is a parallelization level.

Summarizing the above, we can estimate the total execution time using several variables depending on the problem. In the case of TT-count limited scenario, the execution time for SELECT operation is about 15​d​[μ​s]×4​L=60​d​L​[μ​s]15d~{\rm[\mu s]}\times 4L=60dL~{\rm[\mu s]}. In the case of TT-depth limited case, the execution time for SELECT operation is 10​[μ​s]×4​L/b=40​L/b⁡[μ​s]10~{\rm[\mu s]}\times 4L/b=40L/b~{\rm[\mu s]}, which is b​dbd times smaller than the TT-count limited case. Assuming the other parts, such as PREPARE , initial-state preparation, and quantum Fourier transform, are negligible compared to the SELECT, the whole execution time can be estimated by multiplying 2m2^{m} (or number of repetitions determined as r=π​λ/2​ϵr=\pi\lambda/2\epsilon as discussed in Sec. 4) to that for SELECT.

Finally, we verified our analysis with numerical calculation. We have synthesized the quantum circuits of SELECT operations with and without parallelization, allocated logical qubits as shown in the floor plan, determined the routing of lattice surgery with depth-first search algorithms, and calculated the required code beat for SELECT circuits with simulation. The observed coded beats to finish SELECT operations are plotted as a function of problem sizes and the type of Hamiltonians in Fig.S24.

In the numerical simulation, we used the following approximations to simplify the evaluation:

  • •

    We assumed each magic-state factory generates a single magic state per 15 code beat. Note that this value may be improved by using more efficient magic-state distillation strategy, such as the construction proposed in Ref. [103, 106].

  • •

    When Clifford operations are conditioned by previous measurement outcomes, the operations are error-corrected and become available after 1 code beat.

  • •

    While logical SS gates are required after TT-gate teleportation with only probability of 0.5, we pessimistically assume that the logical SS gate is always required.

  • •

    Due to the implementation of PREPARE, LL Hamiltonian terms are not necessarily assigned to the computational basis from |0⟩\ket{0} to |L−1⟩\ket{L-1} in the control qubits. Nevertheless, we assumed it is enough to iterate from 00-th to L−1L-1-th for simplicity. The conciliation between the cost of SELECT and PREPARE is future work.

According to the numerical results, when we do not perform parallelization and only have a single factory (solid blue line), the runtime is close to the product of the rate of magic-state generation and TT-count (broken black line). When the number of factories increases to 44, the runtime saturates at about half of TT-count limited estimation (solid green line). Compared to the depth of circuit (black dotted line), it is about 1.21.2 times larger. We expect that this discrepancy comes from the latency of reactions or path conflicts. When we employ parallelization, the runtime can be reduced to a smaller value while it requires a larger number of qubits and factories. With four threads and 16 factories, the runtime can be suppressed to 0.10.1 times smaller values.
